clinicalPearls: Characterised by a tetrad of blepharophimosis (horizontally short palpebral fissures), severe ptosis, epicanthus inversus, and telecanthus
Inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and caused by mutations in the FOXL2 gene
Type I is associated with premature ovarian insufficiency in affected females, whereas type II involves the eyelids alone
Levator palpebrae function is typically poor, so children often adopt a chin-up head posture to see beneath the ptotic lids
Frontalis (brow) suspension is usually needed for the ptosis because levator function is inadequate
Staged oculoplastic correction commonly addresses the telecanthus and epicanthus first, followed later by ptosis surgery
Amblyopia may result from the ptosis, refractive error, or strabismus and must be screened for and treated
Genetic counselling and, in females, endocrine assessment of ovarian function are important parts of care
reference.pathophysiology: The syndrome arises from mutations in FOXL2, a transcription factor essential for eyelid and ovarian development. Disrupted FOXL2 signalling impairs formation of the periocular structures, producing shortened palpebral fissures, dystrophic eyelid tissue with poor levator development, and abnormal medial canthal anatomy seen as telecanthus and epicanthus inversus. Because FOXL2 also governs maintenance of ovarian follicles, mutation types that abolish its ovarian function additionally cause premature ovarian insufficiency, defining type I disease, whereas mutations that spare ovarian function give the eyelid-only type II phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder with short palpebral fissures
additionalInvestigations: Clinical measurement of palpebral fissure length, intercanthal and interpupillary distances, and levator function
Assessment for amblyopia, refractive error, and strabismus
FOXL2 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and classify the BPES type
Endocrine evaluation of ovarian reserve in affected females, with pelvic imaging as indicated
Family pedigree analysis and genetic counselling
Photographic documentation for surgical planning and monitoring
redFlags: Visual axis occlusion by severe ptosis risking deprivation amblyopia in infancy
Signs of premature ovarian insufficiency in an affected female, such as menstrual disturbance or infertility
Corneal exposure and drying following ptosis surgery
Rapidly worsening compensatory head posture or torticollis
reference.prognosis: Eyelid appearance and function can be substantially improved with staged surgery, though results depend on the degree of levator dysfunction; visual prognosis is good if amblyopia is managed early, but affected females with type I face reduced fertility from ovarian insufficiency.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish BPES from simple congenital ptosis and missing the genetic diagnosis
Not testing for premature ovarian insufficiency in affected females with type I disease
Overlooking amblyopia while focusing on the cosmetic deformity
Attempting standard levator surgery when poor function mandates frontalis suspension
Neglecting genetic counselling for the wider family
references: GeneReviews: Blepharophimosis, Ptosis, and Epicanthus Inversus Syndrome
